principles.title: Figures an organisation can rely on
principles.subtitle: Four habits that come back in my work — and in the projects on this site.
principles.card1Body: Most arguments about a report are about definitions, not about numbers. I pin down the grain and the definition of a figure first, and only then build the model and the dashboard.
principles.card2Body: At the police and in aerospace you work under hard privacy and information-security requirements. Handling information with care is how I start, not an afterthought.
principles.card3Body: Since 2020 I've explained complex technology on Udemy to people without a technical background: 241 students with a 4.2 rating. I do the same with the people who have to steer by a report.
principles.card4Body: Tests on keys and grain, measures reconciled with the warehouse, limitations written down. That is the difference between a nice chart and a figure you can take into a meeting.

open-data-warehouse.title: A star schema on open data, with Power BI on top
open-data-warehouse.sub: A dimensional model on Dutch open data from RDW and CBS: fact tables with an explicit grain, a municipality dimension that keeps its history, and a Power BI report whose measures are checked against the warehouse.
open-data-warehouse.f1Body: Two fact tables with different grains in one schema, each pinned down in a single sentence — because that's exactly where modelling goes wrong.
open-data-warehouse.f2Body: Municipalities merge almost every year. An SCD type 2 dimension keeps a 2016 figure with the municipality as it was called then.
open-data-warehouse.f3Body: The semantic model mirrors the star schema, and the DAX measures are cross-checked against the warehouse: one truth, not two.

ov-streaming-pipeline.title: Real-time delays across Dutch public transport
ov-streaming-pipeline.sub: Delay metrics on the national public-transport feed: per line, stop, operator and network in five-minute windows, shown on a live map that tells you where the network runs late — right now.
ov-streaming-pipeline.f1Body: Every figure has one definition: a five-minute window, a dimension, and count, mean, exact P90, max and min of the delay.
ov-streaming-pipeline.f2Body: Processing the same data twice yields the same windows — correct under late and duplicate events.
ov-streaming-pipeline.f3Body: A Streamlit map of current delays, with Grafana panels that show whether the data behind it is healthy.

about.metaTitle: About me — data analyst with a background at NLR and the Dutch police
about.metaDescription: Data analyst with 241 Udemy students at a 4.2 rating. Set up data-driven working at the Noord-Holland police with data models and Power BI reports, and built dbt transformations and dashboards at the Netherlands Aerospace Centre. Open to new roles.
about.name: Ruud Juffermans
about.intro1: At the Noord-Holland police unit I set up data-driven working in a team that didn't have it yet. I mapped the data sources, assessed their quality, designed the data models and delivered the reports that detectives and managers now steer by. All of that happens under strict privacy and information-security requirements, with data where a wrong conclusion has real consequences.
about.intro2: Before that I worked at the Netherlands Aerospace Centre (NLR) on COMPASS, an EU project on digital product passports. I interviewed partners across Europe and turned their needs into specifications, decided on the data models and structures, built the transformations with dbt and developed Power BI dashboards for the project's stakeholders. My degree in Business Data Management laid the groundwork: data modeling, data warehousing and BI.
about.intro3: Alongside that work I spent four years creating Udemy courses on Python and SQL, among other things. Explaining complex technology to people without a technical background is the entire job there — and it's also what a data analyst does most of the day: explaining what a figure says, and what it doesn't. The projects on this site show how I work, with everything in the open. I'm now looking for a team where I can turn data into models, reports and insights that people actually use.
about.pullQuote: I've seen what happens when everyone steers by the same figure — and what happens when every department brings its own.

modeling.approachTitle: What a team can expect from me

approach.title: Model before building
approach.body: Grain and dimensions on paper first, SQL second. A documented star schema stays understandable after I've moved on.

approach.title: One definition per figure
approach.body: A figure gets one definition, written down in one place. The discussion about what counts happens once, not in every monthly meeting.

approach.title: History stays history
approach.body: Organisations change: teams merge, municipalities redraw their borders. Slowly changing dimensions keep an old figure with the situation as it was then.

approach.title: Tested and explainable
approach.body: Uniqueness, relationships and grain as tests on every change, with documentation and lineage alongside. A model isn't finished until the people using it understand it.

bi.intro: I translate questions from the business into reports and dashboards: the right figure, defined once, on a model that has been checked — presented so that someone without a technical background knows what to do with it.

bi.approachTitle: What a team can expect from me

approach.title: Start from the question
approach.body: Which decision does this figure have to support? I start with the people who will use the report, and only then decide what goes on it.

approach.title: Report on the model
approach.body: The semantic model mirrors the star schema. A report that bypasses the model is a second model — and then you have two truths.

approach.title: Check the figures
approach.body: Measures are reconciled with the warehouse before a report goes out. A data-quality problem goes back to the data owner; it isn't patched in a visual.

approach.title: Explain and hand over
approach.body: A dashboard nobody understands isn't a dashboard. Explanation, documentation and training are part of the delivery.

privacy.metaDescription: Privacy statement of ruudjuffermans.nl, the portfolio site of Ruud Juffermans.
privacy.title: Privacy statement

sections.title: 1. Who I am
sections.content: Ruud Juffermans, data analyst, based in Noord-Holland, Netherlands. This is my personal portfolio site. Email: ruudjuffermans@pm.me.

sections.title: 2. What data I collect
sections.content: Via the contact form: name, email address, optional company name and your message. Via the newsletter: email address. I use privacy-friendly analytics (no cookies, no personal data).

sections.title: 3. Why I collect this data
sections.content: To answer your message and contact you. To send the newsletter you signed up for. To improve the website based on anonymized usage statistics.

sections.title: 4. How long I keep data
sections.content: Contact-form data is kept as long as needed to handle your message, up to a maximum of 12 months. Newsletter data is kept until you unsubscribe.

sections.title: 5. Sharing with third parties
sections.content: I don't share your data with third parties, except where needed to run the site: Proton (email sending) and Buttondown (newsletter). These processors operate under data-processing agreements.

sections.title: 6. Your rights
sections.content: You have the right to access, correct, delete and transfer your data. You can also object to processing. Contact ruudjuffermans@pm.me for any of these. You can also file a complaint with the Dutch Data Protection Authority.

sections.title: 7. Cookies
sections.content: This website doesn't use tracking cookies. No cookie banner is needed.

sections.title: 8. Changes
sections.content: This privacy statement may be updated. The latest version is always available on this page.
